strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: A family of four under continuous cover now needs sixteen agents, and the household that hires them has quietly acquired a second staff
lead.standfirst: Executive protection has repriced since late 2024, and its numbers now sit on the same payroll as the butler's.
lead.body:
Compensation benchmarks published for the 2026 market put an executive protection detail agent in the United States at USD 128,000 at the median base, a detail leader running a detail at USD 185,000, and a vice president of security at USD 230,000. A head of security running a single family programme sits at USD 175,000. The quartiles matter as much as the medians: the same agent role runs from USD 95,000 at the lower quartile to USD 230,000 at the ninetieth percentile, which tells a household that the title alone describes almost nothing about what it will pay.

The number that reshapes a staffing budget is not the salary but the headcount. Continuous cover for a single principal in a static residence cannot be built below five to six agents, because three shifts plus two days off plus one relief is the arithmetic, and the sustainable model is six to eight to absorb training, holiday and unplanned absence. A travelling principal needs eight to twelve, covering the residence, the travelling sub team and the advance work. A family of four at general ultra high net worth threat level requires twelve to sixteen agents, which at the median base produces an annual protection payroll of USD 1.8 million to USD 2.4 million in baseline American markets, and above USD 3 million in New York or Aspen. A yacht above 60 metres carries five to ten, integrated into the vessel's command structure.

This is a repriced market rather than a steadily growing one. The inflection came in late 2024, after which demand for certified protection personnel rose 75 per cent year on year, ad hoc travel security pricing rose 300 per cent, and embedded security provision at the largest contract firm grew 30 per cent. Goldman Sachs Ayco data shows 27 per cent of companies now provide security for their chief executive, a rise of 59 per cent in a year. The supply side has not moved at the same pace, and threat tier is now the single largest variable in pay: a public figure principal costs 1.25 to 1.45 times the baseline, a principal with verified threats 1.55 to 2.10 times.

Geography compounds it. Aspen carries the highest American premium at 1.50 to 1.55 times national base with the thinnest qualified pool of any market, New York and Geneva sit at 1.40, Monaco at 1.35, London at 1.20, and Dubai at 1.10 to 1.15 with the advantage that the income is untaxed. The scarcest seat in the sector is not a protector at all but the technical surveillance counter measures specialist, with an active national pool of twelve to forty people, every one of them trained in a government counterintelligence school, and a median search of 24 weeks.

The failure modes are instructive for anyone running a house. Searches collapse when a principal prices a public figure seat at general threat rates, when a budget for four agents is set against a requirement for 24 hour cover, and when the rota is left undefined at offer stage. Agent turnover already runs at 40 per cent a year, the highest of any security role, and undersized details push that higher within twelve months.
lead.why: The estate or house manager increasingly sits beside a protection programme rather than above or below it, and the two functions share the same gate, the same schedule and the same principal. Reading a threat tier, a rota pattern and a detail size correctly is now part of running the house.

articles.title: Both of the largest business jet makers are now selling faster than they can build, and the family that wants an aeroplane this decade is being told to take a used one
articles.body:
Bombardier closed the second quarter of 2026 with an order backlog of USD 21.8 billion, up USD 4.3 billion in six months, roughly 25 per cent growth in half a year. In the first quarter its book to bill ratio reached 3.6, meaning it booked close to 87 net new aircraft against 24 delivered. Gulfstream's aerospace backlog reached USD 24.0 billion at the end of the second quarter on a book to bill of 1.5, described by its management as the strongest order intake in four years.

Neither company can convert that into metal quickly. Bombardier delivered 56 aircraft in the first half against full year guidance of more than 157, with a heavy fourth quarter skew that has held for three years. Gulfstream delivered 79 in the first half against a raised target of about 160, and 85 per cent of its second quarter deliveries were large cabin aircraft. Build cycles run from twelve to 24 months, so a supplier problem resolved in the spring does not show up in a delivery until the winter.

The secondary market offers no relief. Heavy jet inventory stood at 5.2 per cent of the active fleet in June 2026, below the ten year average of 7.0 per cent and the lowest since February 2023, down 20.9 per cent in a year. Heavy jet transactions rose 43.8 per cent year on year in the second quarter, the strongest quarterly total in a decade, and median resale values rose 13 per cent over the year and a further 5 per cent within the quarter alone. Buyers who cannot find a late model used aircraft are pushed back towards a factory slot that is years out.

The demand behind this is increasingly institutional rather than individual. In February 2026 Vista placed a firm order for 40 Challenger 3500s worth USD 1.18 billion at list prices, with options on 120 more, and fleet operators already accounted for around a fifth of Bombardier's backlog before that order. North American fractional operations rose 11.7 per cent in the first half of 2026. The practical consequence for a private household is that the aircraft it flies is more likely to belong to a programme than to the family, and the availability of a given tail is a scheduling negotiation rather than a given.
articles.why: Whoever builds the principal's travel diary is now planning against a constrained fleet, whether the family owns, shares or charters. Knowing that heavy jet supply is at a three year low changes how early a journey has to be committed.

articles.title: Family offices are cutting property from eleven per cent of the portfolio to eight, and the houses that remain will be examined more closely than before
articles.body:
The 2026 edition of the UBS Global Family Office Report, published at the end of May, surveyed 307 family offices across more than 30 markets with an average net worth of USD 2.7 billion. Eighty one per cent said they intend to adjust their strategic asset allocation, an unusually high share for a group whose defining characteristic is patience.

The clearest single movement is in property. Real estate falls from 11 per cent of the 2025 allocation to 8 per cent in the 2026 plan. Infrastructure moves the other way, from an average of 1 per cent allocated over the past two years to a planned 2 per cent. Artificial intelligence remains the dominant theme, with 65 per cent of family offices already invested somewhere across the chain, from data centre infrastructure to semiconductors, and the leading thematic allocations sit in power and resources at 37 per cent, infrastructure at 37 per cent and AI enabled healthcare at 33 per cent.

Geography is shifting too. North America still takes the largest share of allocations, but offices are actively reducing concentration and planning greater exposure to Asia Pacific, Greater China and Western Europe. The stated reason across the survey is resilience rather than return: geopolitical risk and structural uncertainty are described as reshaping portfolios more than any single market view.

For the private household this is not an abstraction. The family office is frequently the employer of record, the signatory on staff contracts and the budget holder for every property. A three point reduction in the property allocation, taken across a group of this size, means fewer discretionary acquisitions, more scrutiny of the running cost of what is already owned, and a sharper interest in whether a house that is used four weeks a year justifies a year round establishment.
articles.why: Household budgets are set inside the same institution that is trimming its property book. Staff who can present the cost of an establishment clearly, and defend it, are arguing in the language the office is already using.

articles.title: Prime residential growth has slowed to three per cent worldwide, and the gap between the most expensive square metre and the rest has widened rather than closed
articles.body:
Knight Frank's prime international residential index recorded growth of 3.2 per cent across global luxury residential markets in 2025, slightly below the 3.6 per cent of the previous year. The headline number conceals a very uneven map. Middle Eastern markets led the field, driven principally by Dubai, followed by Latin America and the Caribbean, with Asia Pacific and Europe close behind.

Monaco remains the most expensive residential market in the world per square metre, with an average above EUR 57,500 according to the principality's own statistical office for 2025 and 2026. Lakeside villas around Geneva, many of them historic properties with private gardens and their own moorings, reach around EUR 25,000 per square metre at the top of that market. These are not markets that move with the cycle so much as markets that ration supply.

Dubai is the volume story. It recorded 500 residential sales above USD 10 million in 2025, sustaining its position as the most active super prime market in the world. The wider Dubai sales price index fell 1.76 per cent month on month in April 2026 while remaining 6.09 per cent higher than a year earlier, with villas up 9.86 per cent over the year against 5.49 per cent for apartments. A market that is simultaneously softening month to month and rising year on year is a market absorbing a very large amount of new supply.

The pattern matters for staffing more than for valuation. Villas outperforming apartments means houses with grounds, gates and service wings, which is to say houses that require establishments rather than a housekeeper. Monaco and Geneva ration space and therefore run smaller, denser households with older staff structures. Dubai builds them new, at pace, and has to recruit them from outside.
articles.why: The kind of property that is selling determines the kind of post that is created. Villa led growth produces estate roles, apartment led growth produces house manager and housekeeper roles, and the two markets pay differently.
articles.src: Knight Frank, The Wealth Report Prime International Residential Index

articles.title: The secondhand watch index has risen almost ten per cent in a year, and the object a principal hands over most often is worth more than it was
articles.body:
The WatchCharts overall market index stood at USD 38,111 on 5 September 2026, an increase of 9.8 per cent over twelve months. The recovery is real but it is not a repeat of 2021: prices reached a two year high in January and have advanced steadily rather than sharply since, and the market is now generally described as normalising after the speculative period that ended in 2022.

The shape of the recovery is worth understanding. Prices for the so called holy trinity of Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin have stabilised. Core Rolex sports models, the Submariner and the GMT Master II among them, still trade above retail, but the froth has settled into a sustainable band rather than a queue. Smaller case sizes have posted some of the strongest gains of the year, which is a taste shift rather than a liquidity event.

The autumn will test it. Geneva's November sales open on 7 and 8 November with the twenty fourth edition of the Phillips Geneva watch auction, which includes an F.P. Journe estimated at CHF 500,000 to CHF 1,000,000. Sotheby's holds Important Watches on 8 November with a Fine Watches sale running from 27 October to 10 November, and Christie's rare watches sale returns to Geneva in the same window. Three houses selling in one city inside a fortnight is the clearest price discovery the category gets all year.

For a household this is a practical matter rather than a cultural one. Watches are the portable objects most frequently moved, insured, valued, worn abroad and handed to someone else to carry. A collection whose index value has risen almost ten per cent in a year is a collection whose schedule of insured values is probably out of date, and whose travel documentation, customs paperwork and safe arrangements deserve a fresh look before the winter season.
articles.why: Handling, insuring and transporting a principal's watches is ordinary household work, and it is done badly when nobody in the house knows what the pieces are currently worth.

articles.title: Gstaad's first five star hotel, opened in 1910, reopens this winter under Four Seasons with seventy five suites and residences for sale
articles.body:
The Park Gstaad, which made its mark as the resort's first five star hotel when it opened in 1910, reopens in late 2026 as a Four Seasons property. The house will hold 75 suites, along with penthouse residences offered for purchase, in one of the small number of Alpine towns where the private houses outnumber the hotel beds by a wide margin.

The brief given to the architecture is restraint rather than chalet pastiche: warm woods, stone and a limited palette, with a full spa, indoor and outdoor pools and several restaurants designed to keep the property occupied through the summer as well as the winter. Access to the slopes is direct. The residences component, now standard on openings of this kind, means the hotel is also a seller of private property and a manager of it afterwards.

Gstaad matters to private service disproportionately to its size. It is a winter address for families who bring their own staff, and a place where the local supply of housekeepers, chefs and drivers is fixed while demand arrives for eight weeks. A 75 suite opening recruiting through the autumn takes people out of that pool, and every household that winters there will feel it in November rather than in January.
articles.why: A seasonal town with a fixed labour supply cannot absorb a large opening without the private houses competing for the same people. Staff planning for the winter season is now an autumn task.

briefs.t: One hundred and twenty yachts in Port Hercule
briefs.b: The Monaco Yacht Show runs from 23 to 26 September in Port Hercule. Around 120 superyachts will be displayed afloat, of which 43 were delivered during 2026, accompanied by roughly 60 tenders.

briefs.t: London butler pay up a quarter since 2022
briefs.b: Formal butler salaries in London have risen 20 to 25 per cent since 2022, with demand up 9 per cent year on year. British estate managers are benchmarked at GBP 110,000 to GBP 220,000 depending on estate scale, headcount and budget authority.

briefs.t: Burgundy overtakes Bordeaux by traded value
briefs.b: Fine wine indices were broadly flat in the four months to 30 April, with the Liv-ex Fine Wine 50, which tracks the Bordeaux first growths, up 0.7 per cent. Burgundy has taken 27.5 per cent of traded value, moving ahead of Bordeaux to lead the market.

briefs.t: The autumn art diary begins in twelve days
briefs.b: The Armory Show runs from 24 to 27 September in New York with close to 230 galleries, having moved later in the month to reduce the clash with its sister fairs. Frieze London follows from 14 to 18 October in Regent's Park, with the Wednesday by invitation only.
